Parameters: (1) surface geometry — width sufficient for a full folio (typically 40-45 cm), adjustable tilt from near-horizontal to steep; (2) support — a post (fixed, telescoping, or articulated) on a stable base; (3) page-holding mechanism — a clip, bar, or weighted edge that keeps pages from lifting under performer movement or air; (4) mounting class — floor, desk, or wall. Persistence mechanism: manufactured in bulk from wood, MDF, aluminum, or plastic, distributed through retail and music-store channels, maintained through consumer ownership cycles; the form persists as a product category via continuous production, design iteration, and replacement. payload.body: Sheet music is a human-made document bearing a musical score in standard notation: a page or set of pages whose printed, engraved, or digitally rendered marks — staves, notes, clefs, dynamic and articulation marks, and text — encode a musical work, laid out for a human reader at performance distance. Parameters: (1) notation system — the marks follow the shared syntactic rules of musical notation (staves, clefs, note values, dynamics), without which the page is uninterpretable; (2) part vs. full-score layout — a single instrument or voice part or a complete reduction, with system layout and page turns arranged for a performing reader; (3) format — printed or engraved paper of standard sizes (letter, A4, full-score folio) or a paginated digital rendering of the same layout; (4) reading geometry — orientation, margins, and sizing chosen so a performer can read ahead while playing. Persistence mechanism: produced by typesetting, engraving, printing, or digital typesetting; distributed through music publishers, retail, and licensing; maintained through reprints and successive editions; the form persists as a product category, the designed held-object of the music stand. [formal: folium musicum | substrate: matter | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A staff (stave) is a notational structure of parallel horizontal lines — standardly five, with the four spaces between them — whose successive lines and spaces encode successive steps of a diatonic scale, forming the reference frame in which written pitches are placed. Parameters: (1) line count and spacing — the standard five-line staff, with three-line (early neumes) and four-line (medieval chant; modern guitar tablature) variants, the line count fixing how many scale steps are visible without ledger lines; (2) pitch reference — the staff encodes relative scale steps, while absolute pitch is established by a clef placed at its start that fixes a named note to a specific line or space (G-, F-, and C-clefs); (3) system layout — staves grouped into horizontal systems on a page and stacked vertically into multi-part scores (the two-staff grand staff for piano; the four-staff choral score); (4) extension — notes beyond the staff's range sit on ledger lines, short continuations of the staff. Persistence mechanism: standardized since the medieval monastic reform of notation (Guido's four-line staff; the five-line staff by the fourteenth century), reproduced through engraving, typesetting, and digital notation software, and maintained through music pedagogy — the staff persists as the frame within which clefs, noteheads, bar lines, and dynamic markings operate. It is distinguished from musical-notation (the whole symbolic framework), clef (the glyph that keys the staff's pitch reference), and bar (the unit of time delimited on the staff): the staff is the frame, the clef its key, the bar its time, notation the system that contains all three. payload.body: A note is the atomic notational unit of written music: a glyph — a notehead placed on a line or space of a staff, optionally with a stem and flags or beams — that fixes one pitch and one duration. It is distinguished from pitch (the acoustic property the note denotes), staff (the frame on which it is placed), clef (the key that fixes its pitch reference), and bar (the unit of time that groups it). payload.body: A barline is the vertical line drawn across a staff that delimits bars (measures): a boundary mark separating one unit of musical time from the next, by which the beat structure set by the time signature is grouped into the recurring segments the eye can navigate. Parameters: (1) position — drawn perpendicular to the staff lines at a bar boundary, spanning the full height of the staff, and in multi-staff systems the same line links every staff of the system so the boundary is visible across parts; (2) kinds — the single thin line at an ordinary bar boundary; the heavier single line closing a section; and the thick-thin final barline closing a piece or a major section; (3) function — the barline is the mark that makes the bar visible: the bar is the unit of musical time the barline delimits, and the two are distinct carvings (the board's accepted definition of bar names the barline as its visual marker). Persistence mechanism: engraved, printed, or digitally rendered as a mark of the score; sustained through the shared conventions of Western staff notation, the engraving and typesetting traditions that place the mark at every boundary, and pedagogy that transmits the convention from score to score and player to player. [formal: linea barica | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: A human-made element of Western musical notation: a glyph (an arc enclosing a dot) placed over a note, chord, or rest that suspends its rhythm, built to persist as part of the standard notation system through shared performance convention, engraving and typesetting practice, and teaching.

payload.body: A fermata is the notational glyph — a small arc or squared bracket enclosing a dot, placed above (or less often below) a notehead, chord, or rest — that suspends the rhythm at that point: the performer holds the sounding note or the silence beyond its notated value, at discretion, before the flow proceeds. Parameters: (1) form — the standard mark is a curve enclosing a point; textual spellings ('fermata', 'hold', 'al fermata') name the same instruction, and the mark is distinct from the segno, a repeat and navigation marker; (2) application — the mark attaches to a single note, chord, or rest, not to a passage, and is distinct from the tenuto, which sustains a value without extending it; (3) duration — unlike a rest, which fixes a definite length of silence, the fermata fixes no value at all: the hold's length is determined by the performer, the genre's tradition, and the surrounding context, which is precisely why the mark is a suspension rather than a duration; (4) function — the fermata suspends the beat flow at its point of application, producing the rhetorical pause that the score marks but does not measure. Persistence mechanism: standardized in Western staff notation as an engraved, printed, or digitally rendered glyph; sustained through performance convention, the engraving and typesetting traditions that place the mark where the composer writes it, and pedagogy that transmits the instruction from score to score and player to player. [formal: fermata | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.scope: A human-made mathematical function mapping real numbers to positive reals, defined as the power of the base e, built to persist as the canonical growth function of analysis and computation through mathematical formalism, pedagogy, and numerical libraries.

payload.body: The exponential function is a human-made mathematical function that assigns to each real number x the value obtained by raising the base e (Euler's number, ≈ 2.718281828) to the power x, written exp(x) or e^x. Parameters: (1) base — fixed at e, the unique number for which the function's rate of growth equals its value at every point; (2) domain — all real numbers (extendable to the complex plane in the complex exponential); (3) codomain — the positive reals, never zero or negative; (4) equivalent defining representations — the power series ∑_{n=0}^∞ x^n/n!, the unique solution of the differential equation f'(x) = f(x) with f(0) = 1, and the inverse of the natural logarithm, exp(x) = y ⇔ ln(y) = x; (5) fundamental identities — exp(x + y) = exp(x)·exp(y) and exp(0) = 1, which make it the unique homomorphism from (R, +) to (R+, ×). Persistence mechanism: formalized in 18th-century analysis (Euler introduced the notation e^x and the constant e), carried through the calculus curriculum and mathematical analysis textbooks, and implemented in the numerical libraries of every computing environment as exp() under IEEE-754 practice. [formal: functio exponentialis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The logarithm existed and fed into the exponential's formulation; the arrow points from the later object to the earlier source.

payload.body: Priming is the human-made conceptual framework describing the unconscious, non-deliberate activation of specific associations in memory that subsequently influences perception, cognition, and behavior. PARAMETERS: (1) the prime — an explicitly or implicitly presented stimulus (word, image, concept, context) that activates an association, (2) the target — the subsequent stimulus or task affected by the activated association, (3) the interval — the time between prime and target, typically milliseconds to minutes, (4) the match — the semantic, perceptual, or feature overlap between prime and target. PERSISTENCE: priming persists through repeated demonstration in experimental paradigms — semantic priming (cats activates dog), repetition priming (prior exposure speeds recognition), affective priming (prior emotion affects judgment), and procedural priming (prior action facilitates execution). The concept persists as a theoretical construct in cognitive psychology and neuroscience, operationalized through reaction-time measures, priming thresholds, and neural activation patterns. It is distinguished from memory retrieval (conscious recall), learning (stable performance change), and expectation (deliberate prediction). [formal: priming | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
